tour.title: Beyond the Blue and White
tour.subtitle: A digital map of Black history at UNC Chapel Hill
tour.intro: These sites hold Black history that’s easy to miss on a walk across campus. Open any site to find its history, archival images and key people, plus links to the archives behind the story.

welcome.text: Discover the Black history built into the buildings, memorials and sites you pass every day. Tap a pin to uncover who shaped these places, dig into the archives behind them, and reflect on how their stories still shape Carolina today.

tour.mapHint: Explore the map. Tap a location to get more details.

about.description: An interactive campus storytelling experience that connects people to the Black histories, contributions, and communities that have shaped UNC Chapel Hill through location-based discovery, layered digital storytelling, and thoughtfully designed campaign materials.
about.context: Beyond the Blue and White was created at the Visual Discovery Conference 2026 at UNC Chapel Hill.
about.prompt: Highlight Black history at UNC Chapel Hill.

advisors.description: From Chapel Hill, who advised the team on the history of Black labor and community here.

stops.title: Unsung Founders Memorial
history: The Unsung Founders Memorial at UNC-Chapel Hill features a five-foot black granite table supported by miniature bronze figures representing the university’s enslaved and free Black workers, surrounded by five stone stools modeled on Old Chapel Hill Cemetery headstones. A gift from the Class of 2002, the memorial has faced continuous controversy over its design, location, and everyday use.

Community members, and descendants have called its low, two-foot stature a symbol of belittlement and oppression. In 2012, the Real Silent Sam Coalition criticized the monument for honoring a mass of unnamed people rather than specific individuals like Abraham Galloway, Zora Neale Hurston, or Pauli Murray. Further criticism resurfaced in 2021 highlighting the lack of local community involvement in its creation.

In 2019, the memorial was defaced with racist graffiti, and it continues to sink into the ground due to weight and drainage issues, with a recommended restoration yet to begin. Despite these challenges, students and activists have started a new tradition of decorating the monument with flowers to reinforce its intent as a place of remembrance.

people.name: The Unsung Founders
description: UNC would not have grown and thrived without the wealth created by the exploitation of enslaved labor. The joint efforts of researchers, archivists, historians, students, and administrators has resulted in the identification of more than 100 enslaved people who built and labored at the University from 1795 to 1865.

The full history of slavery at UNC-Chapel Hill has yet to be told, much more work remains to be done to better understand the lives and impact of the enslaved people without whom the University we know today would not have been possible.

stops.title: Steele Building
history: Originally built as a dormitory and now an office building, the Steele Building housed the first Black students to live on campus at UNC-Chapel Hill following the landmark legal victory in McKissick v. Carmichael (1951), which integrated graduate education. When Black law students Harvey Beech and Kenneth Lee applied for housing, they were assigned to Room 33 on the third floor of Steele Building, which UNC maintained as a strictly segregated living space—leaving neighboring rooms empty even amid a campus housing shortage.

The students faced widespread social and physical segregation across campus, including segregated seating at Kenan Stadium football games, bans from campus swimming pools, and the cancellation of integrated events like the law school dance. In response, these pioneering students actively challenged the university’s discriminatory policies through direct action and protest—such as Floyd McKissick jumping into the restricted pool to integrate it, and Army veteran James Walker, Jr. lobbying against stadium seating rules and demanding the full rights of democracy.

stops.title: Lenoir Hall
stops.era: Opened in 1940 as UNC-Chapel Hill’s central dining hall
history: Lenoir Hall became the site of a historic worker-led movement in 1969. Organized by Black female food service workers Elizabeth Brooks and Mary Smith alongside the Black Student Movement, two major strikes protested low pay, lack of full-time benefits, and unfair management. The initial strike secured back pay, higher wages, and established North Carolina’s first minimum wage. However, after the University outsourced dining operations to SAGA Food Services, a second walkout was sparked by Smith’s firing, leading to negotiated contracts and sick leave despite ongoing private outsourcing.

This legacy inspired decades of campus labor organizing, culminating in a landmark lawsuit filed by the UNC Housekeepers’ Association. The suit directly highlighted the University’s long history of exploiting Black labor, including the use of enslaved workers and profits made from their sale.

In 1996, the University reached a settlement providing pay raises, bonuses, and the renaming of a campus facility to honor trailblazing Black labor advocates Rebecca Clark and Kennon Cheek. Today, modern student and worker activists continue to call for unfulfilled demands, such as direct compensation and free tuition for descendants of Black campus workers.

people.name: Mary Smith & Elizabeth Brooks
people.description: Mary Smith and Elizabeth Brooks were UNC-Chapel Hill food service workers and labor leaders who spearheaded the landmark 1969 UNC Food Workers’ Strike. Protesting low wages, split shifts, and racial discrimination, they organized co-workers in Lenoir Dining Hall and rallied crucial support from student activist groups like the Black Student Movement. Their months-long strike secured better pay and working conditions for campus employees and ultimately helped spark a statewide minimum wage increase for state workers across North Carolina.
people.imageAlt: Duotone photo of Mary Smith and Elizabeth Brooks at a podium with microphones; Elizabeth Brooks is speaking.

people.name: Marsha Tinnen & Barbara Prear
people.role: Leaders of the UNC Housekeepers Association
people.description: Marsha Tinnen was a UNC-Chapel Hill housekeeper and labor advocate who fought for better pay and working conditions in the 1990s and early 2000s. She co-led the landmark 1996 housekeepers’ strike, which achieved the UNC Housekeepers’ Settlement Agreement, and helped organize UE 150, the UNC Chapel Hill chapter of the North Carolina Public Service Workers Union.

stops.title: The Pit
history: The Pit is a central brick courtyard that serves as a hub for student social life, campus organization booths, and various events—including gospel performances, dances, step shows in the 1990s, and political protests.

In November 1970, it was the site of a tragic event when James Cates, a 22-year-old Black Chapel Hill resident whose mother worked in the university’s campus laundry, was fatally stabbed in The Pit following a campus dance during an attack by the “Storm Troopers,” a Durham-based white supremacist motorcycle gang. Police on the scene failed to provide emergency care or arrest the attackers, sparking decades of community mourning and protest over the University’s response.
After student-placed memorials were previously removed, UNC formally acknowledged Cates’s murder in 2022 by installing an official memorial marker in The Pit on the anniversary of his death.

people.name: James Lewis Cates
description: James “Baby Boy” Lewis Cates, Jr. was born in Chapel Hill October 28 (or 26th), 1948. His father was James “Boot” L. Cates, Sr., his mother was Eula Mae (Trice) Cates. He moved to Chapel Hill High during the town’s integration of public schools in 1967.

Cates never attended the University directly but his grandmother, Annie Cates worked at the University Laundry for decades. In November 1970 he was fatally stabbed at The Pit by the “Storm Troopers,” a Durham-based white supremacist group.

stops.title: Old Chapel Hill Cemetery
history: Old Chapel Hill Cemetery has long been the focus of student and community activism urging the Town and University to address the neglect of its African American section. The section features a tall sandstone obelisk that originally marked the campus grave of UNC’s first president. After a replacement monument was built on campus in 1904, the original obelisk was moved here and rededicated by the Class of 1891 to honor Wilson Caldwell—an enslaved worker turned campus leader—alongside November Caldwell, David Barham, and Henry Smith.

Persistent pressure from Black student groups, including the Black Student Movement (BSM), led to vigils, demands to chancellors, and a 2004 memorial plaque on South Road. Following 2015 surveys that identified 475 graves (361 unmarked), a community effort in 2016 installed a marker honoring Black Chapel Hillians, inscribed with George Moses Horton’s “The Rising Sun.”

people.name: Wilson Swain Caldwell
people.description: A former slave, mentor to students, justice of the peace, elected official, and educator, Wilson Caldwell spent his 57 years working tirelessly for the benefit of his community. Born into slavery as the property of David Lowry Swain—then president of the University of North Carolina—Caldwell went on to become the first African American elected to office in Chapel Hill. His life of service established a lasting legacy that continues to inspire future generations in their pursuit of a better world.
